dailyBrief.text: Good morning — Solon gets the warmest day of the week today: mostly sunny with a high near 76°, though showers arrive early tonight and Friday drops sharply to about 58°. Overnight, Milwaukee finished the job — the Brewers beat Tampa Bay 4-1 in Game 5 to win their first World Series title — and the Cavs rallied past Washington 121-111 behind Evan Mobley's 24 points before heading to Atlanta for tonight's 8 PM tip. In Spain, three days of national mourning begin as investigators ask why a train was authorised past a red signal in the crash that killed 68, and Ohio's election warning is urgent and practical: mail ballots must now be received by 7:30 PM on Nov. 3, so hand-deliver, don't mail. Early in-person voting runs 7:30 AM to 7:30 PM today.

Halloween weekend is packed locally: Solon and Chagrin Falls trick-or-treat Saturday 6 to 8 PM, Jurassic Quest runs Friday through Sunday in Cleveland, and Ohio is offering $15 ride credits in Cuyahoga County all weekend to cut impaired driving. In sports, the Brewers are World Series champions, No. 2 Ohio State plays at USC Saturday night without injured QB Julian Sayin, the 5-2 Browns play at 5-2 Pittsburgh Sunday for first place, and the Cavs' only home game of the week is Monday against Oklahoma City. The standout deal is Giant Eagle's BOGO-free sirloin tip roasts in the ad that starts today — and with the baby due in early November, bags-by-the-door season is officially here.

Spain begins three days of mourning as investigators probe why a train was waved past a red signal
items.summary:
Spain entered three days of national mourning on Thursday for the 68 people killed when two high-speed trains collided near Urda, in Toledo province, on Wednesday morning. Nearly 80 people were injured, 15 of them very seriously. A Renfe train carrying 397 passengers struck the rear of a stationary Iryo train with 147 people aboard; two Iryo carriages derailed and at least three carriages slid down an embankment.

Attention is now turning to a decision made in the minutes before the crash. Transport Minister Oscar Puente said a computer communications failure had triggered a red signal that automatically halted traffic, and that the Renfe train was then authorised to proceed anyway, despite the signal and the stopped train ahead. Renfe says its driver followed instructions, and exactly who decided what is a central question for the investigation.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the scene, promised a thorough inquiry and said any negligence would be brought into the open, while the opposition demanded independent government and judicial investigations. It is Spain's second fatal high-speed crash in nine months on the same corridor, after January's accident near Adamuz killed 46 people — a record that will put the maintenance and signalling of one of Europe's flagship rail networks under harsh scrutiny.

What to watch: service between Madrid and Andalusia remains suspended, and investigators' first findings on the restart decision will shape whether this is treated as a one-off error or a systemic failure.

items.title: Israel's count still produces no winner, with Netanyahu and Eisenkot both short of a majority
items.summary:
Israel's first election since the October 7, 2023 attack ended in deadlock, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor the rival bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot reaching the 61 seats needed to govern in the 120-seat Knesset. Projections through the count kept both camps in the low-to-mid 50s at best, with Arab parties holding a potentially pivotal bloc of seats.

Turnout reached 77.7%, the highest in more than two decades, and Arab parties surged on record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel. That arithmetic is awkward for both sides: Netanyahu's allies rule out governing with Arab parties, and Eisenkot has all but ruled it out too. Netanyahu called for a strong right-wing national government, while Eisenkot argued voters had withdrawn Netanyahu's mandate and urged him to retire.

The stalemate leaves Netanyahu in place as caretaker prime minister while coalition talks grind on, prolonging uncertainty over Gaza, Iran and regional diplomacy. Options on the table range from a unity government to a minority government, cross-bloc defections, or yet another election.

What to watch: once results are certified, President Isaac Herzog begins consultations and gives one leader the first chance to build a coalition — a process that could take weeks.

items.title: North Korea fires about 10 ballistic missiles into the sea as border tensions with the South rise
items.summary:
North Korea launched around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea's military said. The missiles were fired at about 12:30 p.m. from near the coastal city of Wonsan and each flew roughly 250 kilometres. Japan said no missile appeared to land inside its exclusive economic zone.

Seoul convened an emergency national security meeting and condemned the launches as a serious violation of U.N. Security Council resolutions, while saying it was stepping up surveillance and sharing information closely with the United States and Japan. It was North Korea's first ballistic launch since October 12, in a year that has already seen more than 10 test days.

The firing lands in the middle of a sharper border standoff. Tensions have climbed since September mine explosions in the Demilitarized Zone wounded three South Korean soldiers — Seoul blames Pyongyang, which denies it — and North Korea has positioned artillery near the border and threatened to switch on propaganda loudspeakers along the frontier by the end of October.

What to watch: whether Pyongyang meets its own loudspeaker deadline in the next two days, and whether Seoul's proposals for military talks get any response.

items.title: Uganda says 27 of its citizens are dead or presumed dead after enlisting to fight for Russia in Ukraine
items.summary:
Twenty-seven Ugandans who enlisted to fight for Russia in Ukraine have been killed or are presumed dead, according to a letter from Uganda's embassy in Moscow that Reuters saw on Thursday. The embassy named 11 men confirmed dead and 16 more whose bodies could not be found anywhere, including among prisoners of war.

The embassy said the information came from Russia's foreign ministry through a formal diplomatic note, and a Ugandan foreign ministry official confirmed the letter is genuine. Russia's embassy in Kampala did not immediately comment.

The disclosure puts a concrete toll on a recruitment pipeline that has angered governments across Africa. Ukraine has said more than 1,400 citizens from three dozen African countries are fighting alongside Russian forces, some recruited through deception — men promised ordinary jobs who ended up on the front lines. Russian authorities deny illegally recruiting African citizens.

What to watch: how Uganda's government responds publicly, whether families get identification and repatriation of remains, and whether other African governments publish tolls of their own.

items.title: Up to 50,000 people flee fighting in Ethiopia and cross into Kenya, straining aid around Moyale
items.summary:
As many as 50,000 people have fled clashes in southern Ethiopia and crossed into Kenya in about a week, the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said, citing local authority figures. The estimate jumped from 36,000 a day earlier, and officials stress the number is still moving as registration continues.

The fighting pits forces from Ethiopia's Somali and Oromia regions against each other around Moyale. Many of those arriving in Kenya's Marsabit County are women and children; some are staying with relatives, while others are sheltering in schools and churches. Aid agencies list food as the most urgent need, followed by drinking water, shelter, sanitation and healthcare.

UNHCR has sent an emergency team to Moyale and is moving in household supplies and shelter materials for nearly 12,000 people to start, working with Kenyan authorities, the Red Cross and other U.N. agencies. Insecurity on the Ethiopian side has already forced some aid partners to suspend work there.

What to watch: whether crossings push past 50,000, and whether supplies can scale up fast enough beyond the first 12,000 people aid is currently organised for.

items.title: A short U.S.-brokered ceasefire holds in a besieged Ukrainian town, raising hopes aid can get in
items.summary:
A six-day ceasefire brokered by the United States was holding on Thursday around Oleshky, a Russian-controlled Ukrainian town whose trapped residents have endured regular shelling and severe shortages of food and medicine. Neither side had reported a violation since the truce took effect early Tuesday, and demining work was under way.

Russia's human rights commissioner travelled toward the town with a small team of U.S. journalists, while her Ukrainian counterpart headed to the area as well — a rare moment of parallel movement by officials from both countries. The Kremlin said it hoped aid could reach residents safely on Thursday or Friday and that anyone wishing to leave would be able to do so.

The truce, brokered with the involvement of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo, covers Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region. It is deliberately local: fighting elsewhere in Ukraine has continued, underlining that this is a humanitarian corridor, not a wider peace.

What to watch: whether aid convoys and evacuations actually move inside the six-day window, and whether a successful local truce becomes a template — or stays a one-off.

items.title: Trump rallies in South Carolina as a Senate seat his party expected to hold becomes a toss-up
items.summary:
President Trump rallies in South Carolina on Thursday — his second visit in two weeks — because a Senate seat Republicans expected to keep is now rated a toss-up. Incumbent Republican Darline Graham faces Democrat Annie Andrews in the race for the seat once held by Graham's brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July.

South Carolina has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since Fritz Hollings, who served until 2005. Andrews has picked up endorsements from former governors of both parties, while former Governor Nikki Haley has endorsed neither candidate. Graham, Lindsey Graham's longtime political adviser, brushes off criticism of her unpolished campaign by saying she is not a career politician.

The scramble in the South is diverting Republican money and attention from planned challenges in Michigan, Georgia and Minnesota. Republicans are defending Senate seats across seven competitive states to protect a six-seat majority, analysts favour Democrats to retake the House, and Senate control is rated too close to call.

What to watch: Trump closes the campaign with rallies in Florida, Kansas and Iowa before Tuesday's vote — and whether his personal presence moves a race this close.

items.title: Justice Department says FBI and ICE agents will not serve as poll monitors in the midterms
items.summary:
The Justice Department said late Wednesday that no FBI or ICE employees will serve as monitors during the midterm elections. The commitment came in a court filing in a case brought by the NAACP, which sued to keep law-enforcement personnel away from polling places, arguing the plan amounted to voter intimidation.

Instead, monitors will come from the Federal Bureau of Prisons, the ATF and the DEA. The filing says they will act as observers rather than law enforcement: mainly watching and taking notes, barred from carrying firearms, trained not to interfere with voting and instructed to follow state and local rules, consistent with past practice.

The clarification lands against a broader backdrop of aggressive federal election oversight, including administration pressure on states to hand over voter-registration data. Some state officials told Reuters earlier this month they are preparing for possible federal interference in the vote.

What to watch: how the NAACP case proceeds, and whether the monitors' limited role holds in practice on Election Day.

items.title: Federal judge blocks the Justice Department from setting aside 20,000 California ballots
items.summary:
A federal judge on Wednesday refused to let the Justice Department intervene in California's mail-ballot counting to segregate up to 20,000 ballots while voters' citizenship was vetted. Judge David O. Carter warned the move would wreak havoc on an election already under way, in a 26-page order.

The department built its emergency case on a purchased voter list matched against other government data. Carter called that procedure rife with uncertainty and errors, said it would chill voters and discard citizens' ballots, and noted the government already has a tool for genuine cases: prosecuting noncitizens who vote unlawfully. Local officials' early checks found many flagged names were not on the rolls at all, and some flagged as likely noncitizens appear to be U.S.-born.

The Justice Department appealed the same evening. An earlier round at the 9th Circuit sent the case back as premature, with the majority also signalling the department's arguments were likely to fail.

What to watch: the appeal's pace — with counting already running, any reversal would have to arrive fast to matter, making this case a test of how far the department can go inside a state's count.

items.title: Farmers help fund $3 million in attack ads against Republicans in rural midterm races
items.summary:
Farmers are among the funders behind $3 million in attack ads aimed at Republicans in competitive rural midterm races. The ads, running in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Colorado and Iowa, come from the political arm of the American Meat Producers Association, a group founded in 2025 for farmers backing higher animal-welfare standards.

Four incumbents are targeted for supporting the Save Our Bacon Act, which would overturn California and Massachusetts animal-welfare laws. But the spots range wider — one hits a Colorado congressman over tariffs and the Iran war driving prices up. Federal filings show about $2.5 million of the spending opposes Iowa Representative Ashley Hinson's Senate bid alone.

The ads tap real rural strain: record diesel prices, pricier fertiliser and lost exports to China. The administration plans $8 billion in diesel aid, lifting farm payments to a record $55.4 billion this year — but the money arrives after the election. Reuters/Ipsos polling puts Trump's rural approval at a new low of 45%.

What to watch: the group also spent backing two Republican incumbents who opposed the bacon act, so its scorecard is about the issue, not the party — a pattern worth watching in farm country results.

items.title: Trump touts factories, power plants and payouts on the trail — Reuters finds many are years away or uncertain
items.summary:
Campaigning for Republicans in tight races, President Trump has touted billions of dollars in factories, energy projects and jobs, along with cash promises tied to Republican victories. A Reuters review found several of the headline projects remain uncertain, unfunded or years from producing benefits.

In Iowa, the steel complex promoted as a $15 billion project is not expected to start production until 2030, has no finalised state deal and is still securing funding, despite more than $1.3 billion in approved state incentives. A North Carolina quartz investment announced as hundreds of millions turned out to be $56 million, subject to further approvals. South Korea has made no decision on the $54 billion Alaska gas pipeline investment the president heralded, and a pledged $100 million for a Kentucky drug plant was news to the governor's office.

The White House defends the president's record on investment and manufacturing, and the pitch is aimed squarely at voters frustrated by the cost of living. A promised $5,000 dividend for every adult, however, would need Congress — where it has gained little traction.

What to watch: whether voters credit announcements or their grocery and fuel bills when they decide control of Congress on Tuesday.

items.title: Trump rallies in Chillicothe for Husted and Ramaswamy as both Ohio races tighten
items.summary:
President Trump made his third Ohio stop of the cycle on Wednesday night, rallying in Chillicothe for Senator Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. It is a state Trump has won three times, most recently by 11 points — which makes the tightness of both races the story.

Husted, appointed to serve out Vice President JD Vance's Senate term, is locked in a close race with former Senator Sherrod Brown's comeback bid. In the governor's race, polling suggests Democrat Amy Acton may hold a slight lead, and forecasters have shifted it from toss-up toward leaning Democratic amid backlash over a Ramaswamy ad featuring Acton's estranged mother — an ad Trump defended at the rally.

The headwinds are local and concrete: gas prices tied to the Iran war, spiking property taxes and fights over data centers. Trump also urged a yes vote on Issue 3, which would write Ohio's photo ID voting requirement into the state constitution, and hinted Ohio could land a U.S. Space Academy if Husted wins.

What to watch: Ohio turnout in the final early-voting weekend — both parties are treating the state as a bellwether for Tuesday.

items.title: Microsoft beats forecasts as Azure cloud revenue jumps 48%
items.summary:
Microsoft cleared Wall Street's bar comfortably, reporting quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19% and ahead of the $90.75 billion expected. The headline number was Azure: the cloud business brought in $33.2 billion, up 48% year over year — the first time Microsoft has disclosed Azure revenue in dollars rather than just a growth rate.

Earnings of $4.89 a share, excluding the OpenAI investment effect, beat the $4.72 forecast, and the stock rose nearly 4% after hours. Spending came in lighter than feared at $45.2 billion, partly because third-party data-center capacity arrived late, and the company trimmed its expected calendar-2026 capital spending to about $170 billion.

Finance chief Amy Hood guided Azure growth to accelerate to 49–50% next quarter, saying customer demand continues to exceed available supply. Total revenue guidance of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter also topped expectations.

What to watch: Microsoft is becoming the market's proof case that AI spending can pay for itself — the contrast with Alphabet's results the same day (see below) is driving the whole tech trade.

items.title: Alphabet sinks as AI spending burns $9 billion in cash, even as Google Cloud doubles
items.summary:
Alphabet posted a rare double disappointment: revenue of $127.6 billion missed the $128.2 billion estimate, advertising came in $1.4 billion light, and free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion — a second straight negative quarter after a $5.9 billion burn last quarter, for a company that had not posted a negative reading in 22 years as a public company. Shares fell about 10% after hours.

The soft spot was search advertising, where executives partly blamed growing use of AI Mode — the chatbot-style search where ads are still experimental. Net income fell 25% and adjusted earnings missed their target, even as the company unveiled its new Gemini 4 Carbon model the same day.

The paradox is that Google Cloud was booming: revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion, the backlog swelled to $561 billion, and sales of Google's own TPU chip systems are becoming a real business. But finance chief Anat Ashkenazi warned 2027 spending will rise significantly from this year's $195–205 billion plan, with more margin pressure ahead.

What to watch: investors are no longer asking whether AI demand is real — they are asking which giants can fund the buildout without torching their cash flow.

items.title: Nasdaq futures slide as mixed Big Tech results test the AI trade, with the Fed on hold
items.summary:
Tech stocks were set for a rough Thursday morning: Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.22% before the bell while Dow futures actually rose, a split that captures the moment — this is an AI-stock problem, not a whole-market one. Alphabet dropped 10.5% premarket on its cash burn, while Microsoft climbed 3.5% on its cloud beat.

The selling spread through software and chips. Fortinet tumbled 25% and ServiceNow 19% after disappointing results, Marvell fell 9.4% on reports it is in advanced talks to buy optics maker Lumentum, and Nvidia, AMD and Intel all traded lower.

Behind the earnings, the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday, pausing until after next week's midterms while it waits for more inflation data. Traders now see a strong chance of a December rate hike — an unusual backdrop of a central bank leaning toward tightening while tech valuations wobble.

What to watch today: the September PCE inflation report, the Fed's preferred gauge, plus a first read on third-quarter GDP — and Amazon and Intel earnings after the close.

items.title: Chinese AI firms DeepSeek and Moonshot reportedly trained their models on OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra outputs
items.summary:
Chinese AI developers DeepSeek and Moonshot AI relied heavily on outputs from OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model to train their latest systems, The Information reported, in a story relayed by Reuters on Thursday. The technique is called distillation: using a stronger model's answers as teaching material for a cheaper model of your own.

Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro, released last week, and DeepSeek's V4.1-Flash update from October 17 both reportedly benefited from distilling Astra. None of the three companies immediately commented. In a September blog post, OpenAI had already linked a distillation campaign that began in July to individuals associated with Moonshot.

American labs argue the practice lets rivals reproduce frontier capabilities far faster and cheaper than building them, and it has become a genuine flashpoint in U.S.–China technology competition. Anthropic said this month its countermeasures have cut data harvested in distillation attempts by roughly 90% to 99%.

What to watch: whether Washington treats distillation as an export-controls problem — and whether labs can technically prove where a rival model's knowledge came from.

items.title: SK Hynix posts record profit and plans a $75 billion shareholder return as AI memory demand surges
items.summary:
South Korea's SK Hynix, a key Nvidia supplier, reported a record quarterly operating profit of 83.3 trillion won — more than seven times a year earlier and well above forecasts. Revenue rose 328% to 104.6 trillion won, the company's first quarter ever above 100 trillion.

The driver is high-bandwidth memory, the specialised chips AI processors are starved for. SK Hynix says it has sold out of HBM and DRAM until 2029, demand for HBM is running at double its supply, and it expects a chip shortage to last through 2030. It holds almost half the global HBM market and has long-term deals with 14 major customers covering more than half of its 2027–2028 capacity.

Shareholders are sharing the windfall: about 100 trillion won — roughly $75 billion — in dividends and buybacks this year. SK Hynix shares jumped 11% on the report and Samsung gained 9%, lifting Asian tech broadly.

What to watch: with memory sold out years ahead, the bottleneck for AI data centers is shifting from processors to the chips around them — and pricing power is shifting with it.

items.title: Oracle says cash flow turns positive in late fiscal 2028 and tops $30 billion in fiscal 2029
items.summary:
Oracle used its Investor Day on Wednesday to give anxious shareholders a date: free cash flow turns positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and exceeds $30 billion in fiscal 2029. The stock responded with its best day in about five months, closing up 10.73%.

The company guided fiscal 2027 sales to at least $90 billion, up from a record $67.4 billion, and reaffirmed a fiscal 2030 revenue target of at least $225 billion. It capped additional fundraising through May 2030 at $20 billion, split between equity and debt, and said vendor financing, customer-supplied hardware and prepayments will ease its upfront cash needs, with capital spending peaking in fiscal 2027–28 before stepping down.

The reassurance was needed: Oracle's shares had fallen about 50% over the past year on debt-funded AI data-center spending, and its credit rating was cut this year to one notch above junk.

What to watch: Oracle is the leveraged bet in the AI buildout — if its cash-flow timetable slips, both the stock and its credit rating are exposed.

items.title: Pennsylvania measles cases climb close to 1,400 in the state's worst outbreak in years
items.summary:
Pennsylvania's measles count rose to 1,398 on Wednesday, up 38 from Monday's update, in what the state health department describes as its worst outbreak in years. Measles-related hospitalisations in the state stand at 265 so far in 2026, and Pennsylvania has reported five measles-related deaths this year.

The state is the centre of a national surge: CDC data as of October 22 counted 4,588 measles cases across the United States this year, with Pennsylvania accounting for well over a quarter of them in the CDC's tally. The CDC has said it will deploy additional support to help Pennsylvania investigate.

Measles is among the most contagious viruses known, and outbreaks of this size typically trace back to pockets of low vaccination coverage where the virus can sustain transmission. Each new weekly increase extends the period health officials must keep tracing contacts and watching for spread into new communities.

What to watch: the state's next update — whether the weekly increase is shrinking, which would suggest the outbreak is cresting, or holding steady.

items.title: Federal disaster aid approved for 15 Florida counties still cleaning up after Hurricane Isaias
items.summary:
Nearly three weeks after Hurricane Isaias came ashore near Destin as a Category 2 storm, the federal government has approved a major disaster declaration for 15 Florida Panhandle counties. The declaration unlocks FEMA public assistance for longer-term repairs to damaged infrastructure across counties from Escambia to Jefferson, expanding help beyond the emergency declaration issued at landfall on October 9.

The scale of the cleanup explains the urgency. More than 400,000 customers lost power at the storm's peak, six storm-related deaths were reported, and in the city of Milton alone officials estimate 400,000 to 500,000 cubic yards of debris are still waiting for removal, with local resources starting to run dry.

One gap remains: assistance for individual households was still under federal review, so residents cannot yet apply for individual FEMA aid even as public-works money starts to flow.

What to watch: the decision on household assistance, which determines how quickly families — not just county governments — can start rebuilding.

items.title: Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers and coined 'Sí, se puede,' dies at 96
items.summary:
Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers with Cesar Chavez and became one of the most consequential American labour organisers of the 20th century, died Wednesday at 96, her family said.

As the union's chief negotiator and a relentless strike organiser and lobbyist, Huerta helped win contracts that brought farmworkers job security, healthcare, pensions, rest breaks, field toilets, clean drinking water and protection from pesticides — basic dignities that had been denied for generations. She gave the movement its rallying cry, 'Sí, se puede' — 'Yes, we can' — later adopted by Barack Obama's 2008 campaign, and she helped secure the 1975 California law that first gave farmworkers collective bargaining rights.

Her activism carried real costs: she was arrested more than 20 times and was badly beaten by San Francisco police at a 1988 protest. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012, founded her own foundation in 2002 and was still lecturing into her 90s. A former teacher, she often said she left the classroom because she could not stand seeing children arrive hungry.

What to watch: tributes and memorial plans — and how a new generation of labour organisers, in fields far beyond agriculture, claims her legacy.

items.title: Fire at a South Carolina nuclear site injures one worker, with no contamination reported
items.summary:
A fire at the Savannah River Site in South Carolina on Wednesday left one employee with minor injuries and triggered a 'site area emergency' declaration, the Department of Energy said. The fire, at the site's National Laboratory, was extinguished, and officials said no contamination has been reported. The cause has not been disclosed.

The response was broad as a precaution: the injured worker was taken to hospital, non-essential employees sheltered in place, the FAA temporarily restricted flights over the area, and rail, river and ground travel nearby was restricted.

The Savannah River complex was built in the early 1950s near Jackson, South Carolina, to produce plutonium and tritium for nuclear weapons during the Cold War. Today its mission is the long, slow work of cleaning up nuclear waste and managing nuclear materials — which is precisely why any incident there draws an outsized response.

What to watch: the site's explanation of what caught fire — the key fact still missing from officials' statements.

items.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico expand their lawsuit over White House press access limits
items.summary:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico expanded their lawsuit against the White House on Wednesday, asking a federal judge to stop the administration from barring them from the press pool — the small rotating group that covers the president in close quarters such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One.

The outlets say that even after Judge Timothy Kelly issued orders from September 24 onward requiring their access to be reinstated, they have continued to face retaliation for their coverage. They argue the continued exclusion violates the First Amendment. The White House responded that 'the Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office.'

Pool access matters beyond prestige: pool reporters are the eyes of the entire press corps in spaces too small for everyone, and their reports are shared with all outlets. Restricting who may serve therefore shapes what every newsroom — including the administration's friendliest — can know.

What to watch: whether Judge Kelly treats the alleged continued exclusion as defiance of his existing orders, which would raise the legal stakes sharply.

items.title: U.S. approves a license for an $8.2 billion offshore liquefied natural gas port near Texas
items.summary:
The Maritime Administration has approved a deepwater port license for the $8.2 billion ST LNG project, to be built about 10 miles offshore from Matagorda, Texas. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the approval Wednesday.

The port would host four liquefaction plants with combined capacity of 8.4 million tonnes a year, fed by gas from the Tres Palacios storage hub and the Williams Markham plant through an existing pipeline. Construction is expected to begin in 2027, with operations starting in 2029. Officials say the offshore siting keeps tanker traffic away from congested onshore waterways.

The approval was strikingly fast: the final environmental review took 410 days, described as the fastest deepwater port review in more than two decades. It lands as the United States, already the world's largest LNG exporter with more than 100 million tonnes a year in service, has nearly as much again under construction.

What to watch: the administration also proposed new rules Wednesday to speed LNG projects generally — expect environmental groups to test both the rules and this license in court.

items.title: Ohio mail ballots must be received by Election Day — officials warn mailing one now is risky
items.summary:
Ohio's rules changed this year, and the change bites this week: under Senate Bill 293, most absentee ballots must arrive at the county board of elections by the close of polls at 7:30 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3, to count. The old four-day grace period after Election Day is gone, except for military and overseas voters.

Secretary of State Frank LaRose said on October 27 that it may already be too late to drop a ballot in the mail and count on it arriving in time — partly because the Postal Service does not necessarily postmark mail the day it is received. The safe route now is in-person drop-off; in Cuyahoga County that is the Board of Elections at 1803 Superior Ave. in Cleveland.

Early in-person voting continues through the weekend, including Saturday and Sunday, ahead of an Election Day topped by the Acton–Ramaswamy governor's race and the Brown–Husted Senate race.

What to watch: if you know anyone holding a completed mail ballot, hand-delivery is the advice from the state itself — do not mail it.

items.title: More than 1 million Ohioans have already voted early, beating past midterm turnout
items.summary:
Ohioans are voting early at a pace past midterms never reached. More than 1 million ballots had been returned statewide as of October 27 — nearly 700,000 cast in person and over 491,000 absentee ballots returned — compared with about 818,000 at the same point in 2022 and 736,000 in 2018.

The returned ballots skew unaffiliated, with about 500,000 from voters registered without a party, followed by roughly 365,000 Democratic and 311,000 Republican ballots in the Secretary of State's figures. Hamilton County shows the same pattern amplified, with a larger Democratic share of early returns than in either prior midterm.

Early voting is not a result — parties differ in how their voters use it, and Election Day turnout can swamp the early picture. But a bigger, earlier electorate does mean campaigns are now chasing a shrinking pool of undecided, unvoted Ohioans in the final days.

What to watch: the final weekend of early voting, including Halloween Saturday hours, before polls open Tuesday at 6:30 a.m.

items.title: Cleveland City Council refuses to pay $1.1 million for Browns stadium repairs
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council voted 7–6 against reimbursing the Browns $1.1 million for repairs to the city-owned lakefront stadium, with members openly tying the refusal to the team's planned move to Brook Park. The stadium is expected to be demolished within about five years once the club leaves downtown.

The work itself was unglamorous and essential: a failed sanitary pump, a sewer ejector pump failure, failed pipe insulation and an overhead door, among other projects the team had already completed. Mayor Justin Bibb's administration argued the repairs were necessary to operate the stadium safely and that the existing lease obliges the city to repay the team.

Council member Michael Polensek captured the mood, telling administration officials that residents feel the city was sold out over the move and are unhappy about losing both the team and the stadium.

What to watch: whether the administration pays anyway, negotiates, or lets the dispute head toward a legal fight over what the lease actually requires — with the demolition clock already ticking.

items.title: Ohio offers $15 ride credits in Cuyahoga and six other counties to cut Halloween impaired driving
items.summary:
Ohio is putting up to $15 of Uber or Lyft credit in residents' pockets this Halloween weekend to keep impaired drivers off the road. The Project Plan Ahead credits, from the Ohio Traffic Safety Office, apply to rides starting or ending in Cuyahoga, Summit, Butler, Franklin, Hamilton, Lucas or Montgomery counties, from 5 p.m. Thursday through 3 a.m. Monday, November 2.

The need is documented locally: Cuyahoga County recorded 95 OVI-related crashes over the past five Halloween periods, the most in Ohio. Statewide last Halloween, 19 people died in 19 fatal crashes over five days, 13 of them OVI-related. The programme ran earlier this year — about 1,200 rides over Memorial Day weekend, and 4,226 redeemed credits over Labor Day weekend, when traffic deaths fell 55% versus the year before.

Credits cannot be scheduled in advance, the next batch of codes is released Friday at 10 a.m., supplies are limited, and any fare beyond $15 is on the rider.

What to watch: grab a code Friday morning if your Halloween plans involve a drink — Solon's trick-or-treat crowds and party traffic overlap Saturday evening.

items.title: Ohio leads the nation in ballot fights over AI data centers
items.summary:
The AI building boom meets the ballot box in Ohio more than anywhere else in America. Voters in more than a dozen Ohio jurisdictions will decide 21 separate proposals to delay, restrict or ban data centers on Tuesday — the most of any state, according to Ballotpedia — out of at least 41 such measures across 38 jurisdictions in 10 states.

Opposition is strikingly bipartisan. Organisers cite the enormous electricity and water demands of the facilities, plus health worries, even when developers generate their own power. Industry analysts say restrictions are more likely to steer projects to friendlier towns than to stop them, as developers already face years-long waits for grid connections and rising construction costs. U.S. data-center capacity under construction jumped 48% in the first half of this year.

The highest-stakes local fight is in Sunbury, near Columbus, where a ban on facilities using more than 25 megawatts could derail Amazon's proposed $2 billion development.

What to watch: Tuesday's results will draw the first real map of where Ohio communities will — and will not — host the AI economy.

items.title: Amy Acton fires back in Cincinnati: 'Decency is on the line' in the governor's race
items.summary:
Democratic governor candidate Amy Acton took her sharpest swing of the campaign on Wednesday night, telling hundreds of supporters at Cincinnati's Woodward Theater that her Republican opponent tried to use her childhood as a weapon — and that decency itself is on the ballot.

The rally answered a Ramaswamy campaign ad featuring Acton's estranged mother calling her a liar — an ad that drew criticism from Republicans as well as Democrats. Acton told the crowd she has not seen her mother since 1978, the year she confronted her stepfather in court over his sexual assault of her when she was 12. 'It's not going to work,' she said of the ad.

She was joined by Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and Representative Greg Landsman, who focused on healthcare and childcare costs, and by Aaron Dessner and Bryan Devendorf of The National, who performed for the hometown crowd. A USA Today/Suffolk poll released this week put Acton ahead 48% to 44%, within a close margin.

What to watch: whether the ad controversy is actually moving late deciders — pollsters found a small but real net shift toward Acton among voters who had seen it.

baby.tip: Partner go-bag check: alongside Kelly's hospital bag, pack a small bag for Mike — phone charger with a long cord, snacks and water, a change of clothes, toiletries and any meds — and leave both bags, plus the car-seat base already installed, by the door you actually exit through. Hospitals are marathons for partners too, and a dead phone helps nobody.
baby.fact: A newborn's eyes are tuned for exactly one distance at first: about 8 to 12 inches, which happens to be roughly the distance from a parent's face during a feeding. Faces are the first thing babies study, and high-contrast patterns hold their attention longest.
baby.fun: Tiny prep mission: the Moose introduction plan. Wash one receiving blanket now, let it live in the nursery this week, and after the baby arrives it can come home ahead of you carrying the new scent — Moose's official first briefing, at nose level.
